# A Multi-level Approach to Improve Participation in Low-dose CT for Lung Cancer Screening (Empower LCS): A Single Arm Pilot Feasibility Clinical Trial

**Authors:** Alireza Shojazadeh; Raymond Kao; Thao Pham; Aarushi Madan; Richard Echeverria; Wen-Pin Chen; Victoria Nguyen; Omar Gutierrez; Sunmin Lee; Michael A. Hoyt; Argyrios Ziogas; Tan Q. Nguyen; Hari Keshava; Gelareh Sadigh

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Radiological Sciences, University of California, Irvine, CA, USA | 2University of California, Los Angeles, CA, USA | 3Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 4Department of Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 5Department of Population Health and Disease Prevention, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 6Department of Family Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 7Division of Thoracic Surgery, Department of Surgery, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA.

## Abstract

Lung cancer screening (LCS) uptake remains low nationally. We evaluated the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a multi-level intervention to improve LCS uptake in a pilot trial.

Eligible patients were 50–80, and met 2021 USPSTF LCS criteria. The Empower LCS intervention included: (1) a decision aid; (2) text reminder to encourage LCS discussion with primary care providers (PCPs); (3) PCP notifications on eligibility and barriers, and (4) financial hardship and health-related social needs support. Screening outcomes (LCS discussions, orders, and completion) at 6 months were assessed using medical records and surveys. Changes in LCS knowledge and health beliefs were assessed with surveys.

70 patients enrolled (mean age: 62.5±6.3; 70% male; 1.4% Black, 18.6% Asian, 44.3% White, 35.7% Other). 45.7% were Hispanic, and 41% current smokers. Common LCS barriers included cost concerns (40%, 28/70) and fear of finding something wrong (34.3%, 24/70). All received the decision aid, text reminder and PCP alert. 72.9% of patient reported financial hardship or HRSNs and received support. At 6 months, 71.4% (50/70) discussed LCS with their PCP, 51.4% (36/70) received LDCT orders, and 27.1% (19/70) completed screening (52.8% of those with order). Completion exceeded the national average of 16% (P=0.01). Knowledge and perceived severity changed significantly (knowledge: 1.91 to 2.67, p=0.01; severity: 16.3 to 18.1, p=0.0003). No significant changes were observed in perceived barriers or self-efficacy.

The Empower LCS intervention was feasible and improved LCS uptake. However, only half of those with LCS order, completed screening, suggesting the need for enhanced navigation.

This study is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06000683

## Abstract

The Empower LCS intervention, using decision aid, reminders, and provider alerts improved lung cancer screening (LCS) uptake compared to national averages. However, only half of those with LCS order, completed the exam, suggesting the need for stronger patient navigation and follow-up systems.

## Introduction

Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces lung cancer mortality by 20% compared to chest radiography.1 Based on 2021 United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines, LCS is recommended for patients aged 50–80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit in the last 15 years.2 These criteria expanded 2013 recommendations by lowering the screening age from 55 to 50 and reducing the smoking threshold from 30 to 20 pack-years to reduce disparities in eligibility by race, ethnicity, and sex.2 LCS has been covered by insurers without any patient cost-sharing since 2015.3 However, LCS uptake remains low, with only 9.4% of eligible patients discuss it with providers nationally4 and 16% and 13% undergoing LDCT nationally and in California, respectively, in 2022.5

Barriers to LCS fall into two interrelated categories: provider-level and patient-level. Provider barriers include inaccurate smoking histories within electronic medical records (EMRs), absence of EMR notifications for eligible patients, provider time constraints, and concerns about the potential costs of LCS and subsequent interventions incurred by patients.6–8 Patient barriers encompass financial and insurance coverage concerns, lack of symptoms, fear of a positive result, radiation exposure concerns, and transportation difficulties.6,9–11

Systematic reviews suggest that tailored interventions—such as decision-aids, EMR prompts for primary care providers (PCPs), community engagement, and integrating smoking cessation with LCS—could improve screening uptake.9,12 Supporting this, a recent survey of LCS-eligible patients identified patient-reported preferred interventions, including due reminders, PCP notifications, and educational materials.10 However, most prior studies have targeted single barriers or focused only on patients or providers9,12

To address both patient-level and provider-level barriers, we developed a multi-level intervention, Empower LCS, to improve LCS uptake among high-risk individuals. Informed by the Health Belief Model,13,14 Empower LCS targets patients’ lung cancer perceived risk, severity, and perceived LCS benefits through education, and addresses perceived barriers and enhances self-efficacy via patient reminder to discuss LCS with provider and support for financial hardship and health-related social needs (HRSNs). Empower LCS further addresses providers’ barriers through PCP notification of patients’ eligibility. This study evaluated the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of the Empower LCS in increasing LCS orders and uptake.

## Methods

This single-arm longitudinal pilot clinical trial was approved and monitored by the Institutional Review Board, and all patients signed a consent form along with a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) authorization form prior to study participation.

### Study Population

Eligibility included English-, Spanish-, or Vietnamese-speaking patients, aged 50–80 with a self-reported ≥ 20 pack-years smoking history who currently smoked or quit within the last 15 years, per 2021 USPSTF guidelines.2 Patients were required to have a PCP and a scheduled PCP appointment within three months at an academic, community, or federally qualified health center (FQHC) practice in our Southern California health system. Enrollment was stratified by language (30 English, 30 Spanish, and 10 Vietnamese). Given relatively lower number of non-English speakers, lower research participation among non-white patients15,16, and lower LCS eligibility rates of non-white patients based on USPSTF criteria,17 non-English speakers accrual was slow. Therefore, eligibility for non-English speakers was expanded 6 months after study activation, and the requirement for a scheduled PCP appointment at an affiliated practice was removed. Exclusion criteria included recent chest or low-dose CT within the past 12 months, lung cancer history, Alzheimer’s disease, or being medically or cognitively unable to participate.

### Pre-screening and Consent

Between October 2023 and September 2024, we conducted outreach to 4,749 patients who met age and language criteria and were smokers or had unknown smoking history. For initial outreach, EMR smoking history were not restricted to USPSTF criteria, as prior studies reported 30% EMR smoking history incompletion rate18 and 96% pack-year discordance with self-rerport.6 Outreach lists were generated via EMR query. Patients with emails (n=4,511) received upto three Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap)19,20 invitations. Those without email and a subset of non-English speaking non-responders received phone (n=187) or mail outreach (n=276). To reduce technology barriers, bilingual coordinators conducted in-person outreach at primary care clinics. Interested patients completed a 2-minute eligibility survey to confirm smoking history. Additional outreach for non-English speakers included community events, social media, Vietnamese-language radio and newspapers and yielded 7 responses from patients outside our system. Eligible participants completed consent.

### Baseline Survey

Consented patients completed a 15-minute survey in their preferred language via REDCap, phone or paper (in person or via mail). The survey included validated Health Belief Model measures assessing perceived lung cancer risk (3 items),14 and severity (5 item), perceived LCS benefits (6 items), barriers (19 items),14 and perceived self-efficacy (10 items),14 using 5-point Likert scales. Total scores were calculated by summing item responses: risk (3–15), severity (5–25), benefits (6–30), barriers (19–95), and self-efficacy (10–50), with higher scores indicating stronger endorsement. Knowledge of lung cancer and LCS (8 items),21 was scored by awarding one point per correct answer selected and one point per incorrect answer not selected. The score was calculated as sum of all points (0–8 total score).

Financial hardship was assessed using item#12 of Comprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity (COST)) “My health condition has been a financial hardship to me and my family”.22,23 HRSNs were assessed using four items from Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Screening tool covering food insecurity, housing instability, concerns about transportation or utility needs.24 Demographics, insurance, prior screening history, and health literacy (4-item validated Measure)25 were collected. Health literacy scores were calculated as sum of responses to the 4 items and categorized to limited (score 4–12), marginal (13–16), and adequate (17–20). Patients’ full address and zip code were used to calculate national area deprivation index (ADI) percentile using the Wisconsin Neighborhood Atlas.26 Participants received a $15 gift card for survey completion.

### Empower LCS Intervention

All participants received usual care per their PCP affiliation, which in our health system includes an EMR’s Health Maintenance flag for LCS eligibility, contingent on structured smoking history data availability.

All participants also received the Empower LCS multi-level intervention, informed by Health Belief Model,13,14 regardless of PCP affiliation. The intervention addressed patient-level barriers by (1) LCS education: Patients received a decision aid, adopted from publicly available “Should I screen” website,27 covering personalized lung cancer risk (based on smoking, demographic, and medical history), LCS benefits and harms (e.g., radiation exposure, false positives, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment), follow-up recommendations for positive results, and insurance coverage; (2) HRSNs support: Patients screening positive for HRSNs on baseline survey received a brochure from a national nonprofit organization providing financial navigation support,28 where they could self-refer for assistance; (3) Patients’ text reminder: A text reminder to discuss LCS with the provider was sent within two weeks before scheduled PCP appointment. Given the requirement for having a PCP appointment was removed for non-English speaker, for patients without an appointment, the text reminder was sent within 2 weeks of enrollment. Empower LCS also addressed provider-level barriers by PCP notifications (EMR message or fax) within 2 weeks prior to patients’ appointment (or 2 weeks after enrollment if no appointment) summarizing patients’ LCS eligibility, smoking history, and self-reported barriers from baseline survey.

### Follow-Up Procedures

Six months post-enrollment, patients were surveyed to assess self-reported LCS discussion with PCP, provider order of LDCT, and patients’ completion of LDCT. Patients who discussed LDCT with a provider also rated provider engagement to: (1) help the patient understand LCS, (2) listen to the patient’s concerns about LCS decision-making, and (3) consider what mattered most to the patient in decision-making on 5-point Likert scale. Responses of expected to high effort were categorized as high engagement. Surveys also assessed changes in health beliefs, knowledge and patients’ experiences with intervention components. Surveys were distributed via REDCap email with three reminders. Non-responders were contacted by phone and could complete the survey by phone or mail. Patients who completed the follow-up survey received a $15 gift card.

EMR data were also reviewed for patients within our health system (69/70; 98.6%) to extract LCS discussion, order, and completion.

### Outcome measurement

The primary outcome was a provider order of LDCT within 6 months, assessed via EMR documentation or patient self-report. Secondary outcomes included LCS discussion with the PCP, and receipt of LDCT, measured by EMR and surveys. We further evaluated the receipt of any chest CT (i.e., LDCT, chest CT with or without contrast or CT angiography pulmonary emboli).

Additional secondary outcomes included changes in patients’ health beliefs and knowledge about lung cancer and LCS over 6 months, measured by self-reported surveys. Feasibility of intervention was assessed through successful delivery of intervention, defined as percentage of participants receiving all applicable components of intervention.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report continuous variables as mean and standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables as frequency and percentage. Screening outcomes were compared with national benchmarks were available using one-sample proportion chi-square test. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to assess factors associated with LCS discussion, LDCT order or completion. Given none of the variables were significant in the univariable analysis, only those expected to impact outcomes based on prior literature were included in the model. Multicollinearity among variables was examined. Pre- and post-intervention comparisons of health beliefs and knowledge scores were assessed using paired t-tests. To evaluate the impact of the intervention on barriers, a McNemar test was conducted on matched baseline and 6-month follow-up responses. Data analysis was generated using SAS/STAT software, Version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). A complete case analysis was performed. Statistical significance was set at P < .05 without adjustment for the number of comparisons.

## Results

### Study Population

Of 4,756 patients contacted, 19.4% (922/4,756) responded, and 57.7% (532/922) of responders expressed interest. Among these, 85.3% (454/532) were ineligible for LCS, and 1.5% (8/532) had incomplete surveys, resulting in 70 eligible participants (Figure 1). Participants’ mean age was 62 years (range: 50–77), and 71.4% (50/70) were male. A total of 18.6% (13/70) were Asian, 1.4% (1/70) Black, 44.3% (31/70) White, and 35.7% (25/70) of other races. Further, 45.7% (32/70) were Hispanic or Latino. Table 1 summarizes baseline characteristics.

A total of 98.7% (69/70) participants had a scheduled PCP appointment at our health system within 3 months of enrollment and 95.7% (67/70) participated in their appointment. One participant had a PCP at a non-affiliated practice without a scheduled PCP appointment. All 70 participants (100%) received the decision aid, text reminder, and PCP notification, suggesting feasibility of intervention delivery. Further, 72.9% (51/70) patient reported financial hardship or HRSNs and received support.

Of the 70 participants, 60.0% (42/70) completed the 6-month follow-up survey. Responders and non-responders had similar baseline characteristics, except for comorbidities. Non-responders had significantly higher comorbidity (46.4%; 13/28) compared to responders (23.8%; 10/42) (p=0.048).

### LCS Outcomes

LCS outcomes were assessed via EMR for 69/70 patients with a PCP in our health systems and additionally via self-report for those with follow-up survey. For 1 patient whose PCP was not affiliated with our health system, outcomes were assessed via self-report. At 6 months post-enrollment, 71.4% (50/70) discussed LCS with their PCP, significantly higher than the 9.4% nationally reported rate4 (P <0.001). Further, 51.4% (36/70) received an LDCT order, and 27.1% (19/70) completed screening at 6 months (Table 2). Completion rate was also significantly higher than the 16% national5 (P=0.01) and 13% California completion rates5 (P=0.001). Further, 32.9% (23/70) received a chest CT regardless of its indication. Rates of LCS discussion and completion were significantly higher than national rates.

Of patients who discussed LCS and also completed the follow-up survey and responded to provider engagement questions, most reported high provider engagement: 80.0% (20/25) felt providers helped them understand LCS, 88.0% (22/25) felt the provider listened to their concerns about LCS, and 87.5% (21/24) reported that the providers considered their value in decision-making.

In univariable and multivariable logistic regression models evaluating patient factors associated with LCS discussion, LDCT ordering and completion, no variables reached statistical significance except for comorbidity status, which was associated with a lower likelihood of LDCT ordering in multivariable analysis (OR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.10–0.93) (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2).

### Changes in patient-reported health beliefs and knowledge

Descriptive statistics for health beliefs and LCS knowledge among participants with complete data are summarized in Table 3. Significant increases were observed in perceived severity of lung cancer (16.3 ± 2.7 to 18.1 ± 3.1, p <0.001), and knowledge (1.9 ± 1.0 to 2.7 ± 1.6, p = 0.01). No significant changes were found in perceived risk, benefits, barriers, or self-efficacy (p > 0.05).

Baseline patient-reported barriers to LCS are shown in Supplementary Figure 1. The most common barriers were cost concerns (40%; 28/70), worry about abnormal findings (34.3%; 24/70), concern about follow-up costs (32.9%; 23/70), lack of symptoms (27.1%; 19/70), and no family history of lung cancer (22.9%; 16/70). Among participants with barrier data at both timepoints, three barriers changed significantly post-intervention (Supplementary Table 3). Mistrust in healthcare system increased (35 new reports at follow-up vs. 1 report at baseline; p < 0.001), as did preference to not know screening results (4 new reports at follow-up vs. 3 at baseline; p < 0.001). In contrast, fewer participants cited being a smoker as a barrier (8 no longer reporting this at follow-up; p = 0.02).

## Discussion

In this single-arm prospective trial of 70 LCS-eligible patients receiving the full Empower LCS intervention, 71.4% discussed LCS with their PCPs and 51.4% received an order, exceeding the national (9.4%) 29 and institutional (34.8%) patient-reported discussion rates.10 Further, 27.1% (52% of those with order) completed screening, which is significantly higher than the national (16%) and California (13% ) averages.5 However, stronger patient navigation and follow-up may be needed to support screening completion after an order is placed. Our results align with prior studies that show multi-level interventions can improve LCS uptake. For example, a multifaceted intervention including a shared decision-making tool, clinician reminders, narrative guidance provided in the ordering process, and patient reminders increased LDCT completion from 6.8% to 23.7%.30 These findings suggest the feasibility and effectiveness of our intervention in improving LCS, and offer a model for expanding screening efforts for lung cancer and other radiology-based cancer screenings.

A key strength of this study is its racially and ethnically diverse cohort. Over half (55.7%) of participants identified as non-White, substantially higher than most LCS studies.1,30 This reflects the success of our recruitment strategies in engaging underrepresented populations and enhances the generalizability of our findings to communities that have historically faced greater barriers to LCS and may benefit most from targeted, culturally tailored interventions. While LCS guidelines struggle to balance equal benefit-based eligibility and program sensitivity across racial and ethnic groups,31 we observed no difference in LCS discussion, LDCT order or completion among white vs. non-white participants (Supplementary Table 1). Our study’s diverse cohort underscores the importance of inclusive research in guiding equitable LCS implementation.

System-level barriers to LCS include external policies and incentives, such as reimbursement structures, guidelines-based eligibility criteria, and reporting requirements.32 These factors can hinder uptake when reimbursement is unclear or eligibility is difficult to determine via existing EMR systems. Implementation challenges also include integrating screening into clinical workflows, ensuring staff training, and maintaining consistent EMR prompts. Our intervention addressed some of these by using a study coordinator to assess eligibility through self-reported smoking history and sending EMR-based provider reminders. However, reliance on staff to collect smoking history limits scalability. Improving structured EMR documentation of smoking history is essential to enable automated reminders, streamline workflows, and support sustainable LCS implementation.

Overall, participants reported lower perceived barrier scores at the 6-months (37.5 vs. 40.7 at baseline). However, this change was not statistically significant. Notably, there was a significant decrease in viewing “being a smoker” as a barrier, but increases in healthcare mistrust and preference not to know screening results. The reduction in “being a smoker” suggests decreased internalized stigma or improved understanding that smoking is an indication—not a disqualifier—for screening. This is encouraging, as current smokers are historically less likely than former smokers to follow LCS guidelines.33,34

While Empower LCS improved knowledge and recognition of lung cancer severity, mistrust in the healthcare system and preference not to know screening results increased at 6-months. This unexpected trend may reflect growing awareness among participants of the structural barriers and inequities they face in accessing care, prompting more critical views of healthcare, particularly among those with prior experience of discrimination, poor follow-up, or financial strain.35 Such mistrust could have influenced participants’ engagement with the intervention or followed through with screening, highlighting the complex interplay between trust, perceived barriers, and health behavior. These findings underscore the importance of pairing education with trust-building strategies, such as community partnerships, culturally responsive communication, and opportunities for meaningful engagements with trusted providers.

Our study has several limitations. First, it was conducted predominantly within a single health system, limiting generalizability. However, recruitment spanned 11 primary care practices including academic, community, and FQHC, and included broader community outreach. Second, despite broad multimodality outreach, response rates to outreach were low, consistent with similar studies.36 One reason may be inclusion of patients without confirmed LCS eligibility in EMR. Due to frequent gaps in EMR smoking history,6,37 we invited individuals with unknown LCS eligibility status, which likely led some nonsmokers to disregard the invitation. A more complete EMR dataset could have enabled more targeted outreach and improved response rates. Nonetheless our study provides valuable insight into the feasibility of engaging hard-to-reach populations in real-world settings. Third, 40% of participants were lost to follow-up at 6 months, though baseline characteristics were similar between responders and non-responders, except for comorbidities, suggesting comorbidities may have contributed to attrition. Fourth, since all participants received the full Empower LCS intervention, we could not isolate the effects of individual components (e.g., decision aid, text reminder, provider notification, HRSN support). However, prior meta-analysis suggest multi-component interventions are more effective than single ones.38 Finally, Health Belief Model constructs were measured at 6-month, rather than immediately post-intervention, potentially confounding results due to subsequent LDCT receipt or screening outcomes.

In summary, this pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of a multi-level intervention to improve LCS uptake in diverse populations and highlights the need for larger studies to confirm its impact.

# Reliability of Electronic Medical Record to Assess Patient’s Eligibility for Lung Cancer Screening: Analysis of Two Pilot Trials

**Authors:** Ryan Sabour; Mahnur Bharucha; Rhea Gandhi; Richard Echeverria; Victoria Nguyen; Wen-Pin Chen; Argyrios Ziogas; Sunmin Lee; Tan Q Nguyen; Hari B Keshava; Michael A Hoyt; Gelareh Sadigh

## Abstract

Accurate smoking history documentation in electronic medical records (EMRs) is essential for determining lung cancer screening (LCS) eligibility. We investigated the completeness of EMR smoking data, its concordance with patients’ self-reports, and its reliability for LCS eligibility after 2021 LCS United States Preventive Services Task Force guideline change.

Between October 2023 and November 2024, patients aged 50 to 80 years with a primary care visit in academic and community practices of a health system, who were current or former smokers or had an unknown smoking history based on EMR, and who were being screened for two clinical trials on interventions to improve LCS were enrolled. Participants completed an LCS eligibility verification survey, and EMR smoking data from the most recent visit before PCP encounter were extracted for comparison.

In total, 322 patients were included (mean age 62.4 ± 7.9; 58.1% male; 15.6% Asian, 1.2% Black, 61.4% White, and 21.8% other races; 45.7% Hispanic). Overall, 39.4% (127 of 322) had incomplete EMR smoking history to determine LCS eligibility. Among 167 smokers with both EMR and self-reported pack-year data, 85.6% (143 of 167) showed discordance in pack-year. Further, 26.2% (51 of 195) of patients with determined EMR eligibility (15.8% of 322 participants) had discordant eligibility based on self-report. Hispanic (versus non-Hispanic) patients were more likely to have incomplete EMR data to assess LCS eligibility (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.80) and discordant EMR eligibility with self-report (odds ratio, 2.34; 95% confidence interval 1.10–5.08).

This study highlights significant gaps in smoking history documentation within EMRs, with high rates of incomplete and discordant data, particularly among Hispanic populations.

Keywords: Discordance, electronic medical record, lung cancer screening, self-report, smoking history

## INTRODUCTION

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, accounting for nearly two million deaths annually worldwide [1]. In 2011, the National Lung Screening Trial showed annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening (LCS) in high-risk populations resulted in a 20% decrease in lung cancer mortality compared with chest radiograph [2]. Recognizing the importance of early-stage detection, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) established LCS recommendations in 2013 [3]. Since 2015, both CMS and commercial insurance plans cover LCS with no patient cost sharing. Utilization, however, remains low, with fewer than 16% of nationally eligible individuals undergoing LCS, as assessed by the 2024 “State of Cancer” Report by the American Lung Association [4].

One of the main provider-level barriers to LCS is failure of electronic medical records (EMRs) to notify physicians of patients’ eligibility for LCS [5,6], mainly due to incomplete smoking history documentation in the EMR [6]. Unlike screening for other types of cancer, in which eligibility is largely determined by age and gender, LCS uses a risk-based approach that primarily factors in age and smoking history, including pack-year and years since quitting [7], and therefore, any missing data in smoking history could result in inability to assess patients for LCS eligibility.

Few studies have reported on completeness of EMR in documentation of smoking status [8,9], smoking intensity (ie, packs per day or pack-year) [9,10], concordance of EMR documented smoking history with self-reported history, as well as EMR reliability in assessing patients’ eligibility for LCS [11]. However, all these studies were conducted before the 2021 USPSTF recommendation update that expanded age eligibility from 55 to 80 to 50 to 80, and decreased smoking pack-year eligibility from 30 to 20 and before the American Cancer Society 2023 LCS recommendations eliminating the quit date for former smokers.

Despite national efforts to improve LCS, in a 2023 survey of primary care providers (PCPs) and pulmonologists, inaccuracies of EMR to identify eligible patients was recognized as a barrier to LCS by more than half of providers [6]. Therefore, we aimed at providing an update on completeness of EMR in documentation of smoking status and intensity, its concordance with patients’ self-reported smoking history and its reliability to determine LCS eligibility. Our study offers updated insights following the 2021 guideline, with a unique emphasis on disparities affecting Hispanic patients who are underrepresented in prior LCS documentation studies. Further, we focus not only on completeness and concordance, but also on the clinical implications of EMR misclassification at the patient level.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Setting

This study is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from patients screened for two pilot clinical trials (Empower LCS and Empower Latinx) (clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06000683 and NCT06225414) [12,13] based on data from patients screened between October 2023 and November 2024 at a tertiary academic health center, affiliated community clinics, and Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC). The two studies were approved by Institutional Review Boards 3439 and 4471, and an informed consent and a HIPAA authorization form were signed before data collection.

### Participants

Empower LCS [12] is a single-arm pilot clinical trial, and Empower Latinx [13] is a randomized pilot clinical trial. Both recruited patients eligible for LCS to test feasibility and efficacy of a multilevel intervention to improve LCS. Both trials required patients 50 to 80, who meet 2021 USPSTF LCS eligibility criteria by self-reported smoking history at enrollment and who had a scheduled PCP appointment (index PCP visit) within 3 months at one of our health system 11 affiliated academic, community, or FQHC clinics. The PCP requirement ensured that eligibility assessment was followed by a clinical encounter in which LCS discussions could take place, though prior PCP visits were not required. Empower Latinx trial protocol was later amended (effective 2025, not applicable here) to include patients having a PCP regardless of upcoming appointments. Empower LCS recruited English-, Spanish-, or Vietnamese-speaking patients of any race or ethnicity; Empower Latinx goal recruited English- or Spanish-speaking patients of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity.

Given the two pilot trials had similar enrollment processes and similar eligibility criteria (differing only by participant race or ethnicity) and used the same LCS eligibility verification questionnaire, we combined their data to increase sample size and diversity for the current analysis.

Eligibility criteria for the current study were patients aged 50 to 80 years with an upcoming PCP encounter (index encounter) at any of the 11 affiliated primary care academic, community, and FQHC clinics. All patients were smokers or former smokers or had an unknown smoking history based on EMR structured data and were being screened for participation in Empower LCS or Empower Latinx trials by completing an LCS eligibility verification questionnaire between October 2023 and November 2024.

Exclusion criteria included being a nonsmoker based on EMR structured data, a history of dementia, or inability to participate medically or cognitively, as evaluated by the EMR notes or study coordinator. Additionally, patients who did not complete a HIPAA authorization form were excluded from the study.

At the time of this study analysis in December 2024, Empower LCS was closed to accrual (n = 70), and Empower Latinx was still recruiting (n = 32 of 60 planned). For the present study, we included all Empower LCS participants (n = 70), all enrolled Empower Latinx participants (n = 32), and individuals who completed LCS eligibility verification and HIPAA authorization but were ineligible for the trials (n = 220), yielding a total analytic sample of 322.

### Recruitment

Patient outreach for the two trials was through e-mail invitations via Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) [14,15] with three e-mail reminders in patients’ preferred language based on EMR. In addition to reminders, nonresponders received a one-time text message. Additionally, we used outreach via mail, telephone, and in person in the clinic by bilingual study coordinator as backup for those without valid e-mail address and a convenience sample (30%) of nonresponders as was feasible by study resources.

### Self-Reported Smoking History

Self-reported smoking history was collected via a structured 2-min LCS eligibility verification survey that was aimed at assessing eligibility for enrollment in Empower LCS and Latinx trials. This survey was administered electronically via institutional REDCap [14,15], on paper during primary care clinic visits, or via telephone in patients’ preferred language. The survey inquired about smoking status (current, former, or never smoker), average number of cigarettes smoked per day, total years of smoking, and years since quitting.

### EMR-Record Smoking History

EMR-recorded smoking history including smoking status, average number of cigarettes smoked per day, total years of smoking, average smoking pack-year, and years since quitting was extracted using EMR search function from the most recent encounter with available smoking data that was before patients’ index PCP encounter. If all components of smoking history could not be extracted from a single encounter note, notes from different encounters were used. Extracted data were based on both structured and free text data available in the note. Our EMR has structured fields corresponding to each of the smoking history components outlined previously. Documentation can be completed by medical assistants during patient rooming or by the providers (eg, physician or advanced practice provider), but some providers may instead use free text entries.

The rational for data extraction before index PCP visit was to assess reliability of using EMR data to determine patients’ LCS eligibility before PCP visit. PCP time constraints to verify LCS eligibility and lack of EMR notification are known provider-level barriers [6], and although EMR health maintenance flags are a solution to this barrier, they are often not triggered due to incomplete smoking history documentation. Smoking history data extraction before index PCP visit enables assessing the scope of problem.

### Sociodemographic Information

We further extracted patient sociodemographic information including age, gender at birth, self-reported race and ethnicity, primary language, marital status, employment status, health insurance, and full address and zip code from EMR or self-reported surveys for patients enrolled in Empower LCS and Latinx trials. Area Deprivation Index (ADI) national percentile scores were calculated based on patients’ full addresses mapped to census block groups using the University of Wisconsin Neighborhood Atlas [16,17]. The ADI involves neighborhood socio-economic indicators such as income, education, employment, housing, and health care access. The score ranges between 0 and 100, with higher scores indicating greater socio-economic disadvantage. Index PCP encounter practice type (academic, community, and FQHC) was extracted.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report continuous variables as mean and SD, and categorical variables as frequency and percentage. LCS eligibility based on self-reported smoking history and EMR data were determined using the 2021 USPSTF guidelines [18]. Discordance rate between self-reported and EMR documented pack-year as well as LCS eligibility was assessed using McNemar’s test for categorical variables. Discordance in pack-year was calculated as absolute discordance. We further assessed discordance in LCS eligibility, defined as any difference in LCS eligibility classification between EMR and self-report, regardless of which one classified patient as LCS eligible.

Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to assess patient-level and practice-level factors associated with incomplete smoking history documentation (dependent variable) or discordance between EMR and self-reported smoking history (dependent variable). Covariates for the univariable model included age, gender at birth, race, ethnicity, primary language, marital status, employment status, insurance type, ADI, and practice type. Variables with P <.05 in univariable analyses, as well as those selected a priori based on clinical relevance and prior literature, were included in the multivariable models. Multicollinearity among variables was assessed. Given concern for multicollinearity between language and ethnicity, only ethnicity was included in the multivariable model. A complete case analysis was conducted. Statistical significance was set at P < .05. All analyses were performed using SAS v9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Carey. NC).

## DISCUSSION

Secondary analysis of data from two prospective clinical trials conducted between 2023 and 2024 revealed our institutional EMR was insufficient for accurately determining LCS eligibility in 55.2% (178 of 322) of participants, with 39.4% (127 of 322) having incomplete documentation and 15.8% (51 of 322) showing discordance between EMR and self-reported eligibility. Our study confirms persistent challenges in smoking history documentation that undermine accurate LCS eligibility assessment.

Our study data collected 2 years after USPSTF recommendation update remain similar to the studies conducted before 2021 USPSTF recommendation. In contrast to earlier studies that evaluated EMR documentation before the 2021 USPSTF guideline changes, our study includes an oversampled Hispanic cohort to provide a more nuanced understanding of disparities in documentation. In a 2016–2017 study, Patel et al found 41% incomplete EMR documentation rate and a 23% EMR and self-report discordance in eligibility rate [10]. In another 2014–2016 study, there was 96% discordance between pack-year documented in EMR and self-report, slightly higher than 85.6% reported in the current study [11]. Of note, there was 85% underreporting of smoking intensity (ie, pack-year) in EMR [11], and our study observed both under- and overreporting of pack-year. In the current study, underreporting of pack-year in EMR compared with self-report was more common than overreporting (68% versus 22%) among individuals ineligible for LCS based on EMR, which may contribute to low LCS uptake, as patients with underreported pack-years may not be flagged as eligible by EMR health maintenance tool. Among patients classified as eligible by EMR, underreporting remained the predominant trend (43%), followed by overreporting (39%). Although the survey and EMR information are both patient reported, discordance in the data might be due barriers in patient communication, specifically in cases of patients with limited English proficiency or low health literacy, as well as the temporal effect with EMR information having been recorded earlier than the self-reported survey. We did not document the encounter date of smoking history extraction from EMR and cannot assess the temporal effect. However, if EMR smoking data from prior encounters are expected to be the source data for tools such as health maintenance to address PCP barriers during their encounters, the current status of smoking status in EMR is not reliable.

Our study showed Hispanic patients are more likely to have incomplete EMR data for LCS eligibility or discordance between EMR versus self-reported eligibility. Hispanic patients, particularly those with limited English proficiency, face added communication challenges when provider-patient language discordance exists. Prior study showed only 60% of physicians and 37% of nurses use interpretive services for patients with limited English proficiency [19]. Additionally, encounter with these patients may be shorter [19], potentially limiting EMR documentation and contributing to disparities in screening. Greater providers’ cultural competency and frequent use of interpretive services may help reduce this gap.

Frequent documentation and update of smoking history through previsit questionnaires in the patient portal could improve EMR completeness [20]. In our study population, which oversampled Hispanics, portal use was 48% compared with 61.3% nationally. Therefore, portal questionnaires may not reach all patients, particularly since Hispanic patients are less likely to be offered portal access [20], further contributing to disparities. Another limitation is that smoking history entered in portals often does not automatically populate structured EMR fields and requires manual provider verification, creating inefficiencies. Patients who use portals are also more likely to discuss LCS with their provider [21], but, if providers enter smoking data as free text, it fail to trigger automated alerts or clinical decision support tools. Encouraging providers to consistently use structured EMR fields may help.

A 2023 study showed unstructured clinician notes captured smoking history more accurately than structured entries [22], which were present for only 12.5% of patients. Natural language processing (NLP) applied to unstructured clinician notes identified smoking history in 41.8% of cases [22]. A hybrid approach using NLP to map free text into structured EMR fields, and flag inconsistencies for health care provider review, could reduce manual verification, improve data completeness, and enhance screening uptake [23]. However, implementing NLP across health care systems faces challenges including validation requirements, integration into EMR workflows, and clinician acceptance, and ongoing provider review may still be needed, limiting scalability.

Pay-for-performance programs have shown to improve smoking status documentation [24]. Such efforts can be expanded to include quantitative pack-year tracking, NLP-validated data integration, and increasing LCS rates. Further, implementation of smoking documentation reminders built into the EMR may also enhance completeness, as demonstrated for smoking cessation efforts [25]. Lastly, others have shown an EMR-derived multivariable prediction model can aid in identification of LCS-eligible patients, but this also requires availability of smoking history data in the EMR to feed the model [26].

Our cohort consisted of patients who were interested to participate in clinical trials, which may limit the representativeness of the sample relative to the broader clinic population. As a single-center study, generalizability may be limited by institutional documentation practices. Further, provider documentation practices may vary across departments, influencing completeness. Our outreach response rate was 19.4% despite multimodality outreach effort, which may also impact generalizability. However, due to focus of Empower Latinx trial on Hispanic population, we oversampled Hispanic patients compared with our catchment area. Both EMR and survey data are self-reported, and we acknowledge the absence of an objective reference standard. However, the structured and standardized nature of survey collection—administered by trained bilingual research staff at the point of enrollment using dedicated prompts—likely improved completeness and reduced underreporting compared with routine EMR documentation, which is often updated inconsistently. We did not systematically evaluate whether smoking history was updated after the index PCP encounter as PCPs for patients enrolled in Empower LCS and Latinx trials were actively receiving alerts on their patients LCS eligibility, and hence this may impact their documentation of smoking history within the context of the clinical trial. We also did not control for prior longitudinal PCP relationships. Future studies should evaluate whether enhanced EMR accuracy translates to reduced screening disparities, particularly among populations with historically low LCS adherence.

- This study highlights significant gaps in smoking history documentation within EMRs, with high rates of incomplete and discordant data.

- Hispanic patients are more likely to have incomplete EMR data to assess LCS eligibility.

- These discrepancies pose a direct barrier to LCS eligibility determination and demonstrate a need for systematic improvements in smoking history documentation.

# Maximizing safety of ultrasound‐guided intralymphatic allergen administration in the superficial inguinal lymph node

**Authors:** Min‐Jeong Cho; Victoria Nguyen; Hiroo Suami; Casey T. Kraft; Monica T. Kraft

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Columbus Ohio USA | 2 Division of Allergy and Immunology The Ohio State University and Nationwide Children's Hospital Columbus Ohio USA | 3 Faculty of Medicine, Health and Human Sciences Macquarie University Sydney New South Wales Australia | 4 Columbus Cosmetic Columbus Ohio USA | 5 Department of Otolaryngology, Division of Allergy and Immunology The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center Columbus Ohio USA

To the Editor,

Traditionally, subcutaneous immunotherapy has been the gold standard method of inducing immune response to tolerance and desensitization of allergen extract for the treatment of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Since the first clinical trial of intralymphatic immunotherapy (ILIT) was published nearly two decades ago, 1 ILIT has emerged as an alternative choice due to its ability to deliver antigen locally while minimizing risk of systemic adverse reactions and inducing a rapid onset of effect. Several studies have shown the safety and efficacy of the ILIT therapy for seasonal and perennial allergy symptoms by targeting a variety of superficial lymph node regions, including inguinal, cervical and tonsillar. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 Recently, Flory et al. presented practical recommendations on ultrasound‐guided injections based on a review of videos of 173 ILIT injections performed at their institution. 6 In addition to considerations of sonographic and injection technique, we wish to highlight to importance of a careful understanding of lymphatic anatomy and selection of the targeting lymph node prior to incorporating this procedure into clinical practice.

The lymphatic system is divided into lymphosomes, which consist of superficial lymph‐collecting vessels and their corresponding lymph nodes. 7 As each lymphosome is responsible for the regional maintenance of fluid balance, any inadvertent injuries to regional lymph nodes can lead to lymphedema, a chronic debilitating condition that leads to negative functional, esthetical, and physical impact in patient's lives. 8 Therefore, knowledge of the normal anatomy of the lymphatic system and the potential cause of lymphedema by its damage is crucial for those who are practicing ILIT.

Typically, critical structures including the inguinal/femoral arteries and veins are identified and the region lateral to the vessels are scanned to identify a suitable lymph node in the inguinal ILIT. In the inguinal region, there are three subgroups of the superficial lymph nodes: the abdominal, lateral thigh, and medial thigh groups (Figure 1). 9 It is critical to prevent injuries to the medial thigh group as the majority of lymph vessels originating from the feet drain to two or three dominant lymph nodes of this group, which is bordered by the inguinal ligament, the medial border of the sartorius, and the lateral border of the adductor longus. As this procedure gains popularity in clinical use, it is important to acknowledge that these superficial nodes have important functionality. Currently, microsurgeons harvest superficial inguinal lymph nodes to autograft them for the treatment of lymphedema while carefully preserving the deep lymph nodes for the lower extremity via reverse groin lymph node mapping and preoperative SPECT CT. Microsurgeons utilize high‐frequency ultrasound to identify the precise location of superficial lymph nodes to prevent the injury of deep lymph nodes, reducing the risk to ~1.5%. 10 While there are limited studies on the frequency of the ultrasound probe used in ILIT, the majority of the portable ultrasound probe has a low frequency (1‐10 Mhz), compared to 48–70 Mhz used in ultrasound mapping for lymphedema, which provides significantly less anatomic details (Figure 2).

To conclude, ILIT represents a promising advancement in the administration of aeroallegen immunotherapy for rhinoconjunctivitis by offering localized delivery, minimizing risk of anaphylaxis and significantly reducing treatment period compared to traditional immunotherapy. While the small clinical trials to date support the safety and efficacy of this treatment, popularizing clinical use amongst allergists, there is a lack of dedicated anatomic studies and further studies should be completed to address anatomic considerations of the lymph node regions. High frequency ultrasound use should be considered to optimize visualization of lymph nodes to minimize risk of iatrogenic lymphedema which has been observed in other specialties.
